title: Ruth
subtitle: faithful love in the days of the judges
lead: Ruth is a short story, four chapters long, about two widows and a harvest. Naomi, an Israelite who has lost her husband and both sons in Moab, comes home to Bethlehem bitter and empty. Ruth, her Moabite daughter-in-law, refuses to leave her: "Your people are my people, and your God is my God" (1:16). In the fields of a relative named Boaz, Ruth finds food, protection and, in the end, a husband. Their son Obed becomes the grandfather of King David.

God works almost entirely out of sight. The narrator says only twice that the LORD acted (1:6; 4:13), yet the "chances" keep falling in the right place. The book's key word is hesed, faithful love that goes beyond what duty requires, and it is shown most of all by the foreigner.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Talmud, Bava Batra 14b) says Samuel. Most scholars think the author is unknown.
Set about 1100 BC, in the days of the judges. Written between the time of David (about 1000–950 BC) and the 400s BC; scholars are divided.
Moab, east of the Dead Sea, and Bethlehem in Judah
A short story with a closing genealogy (4:18–22). Traditionally read as history; many scholars call it a historical novella, an idyll or a folktale.

audience.to: Israelites in Judah who lived well after the story's time. The book is set "In the days when the judges ruled" (1:1). It explains an old custom its readers no longer knew (4:7). It ends with a family line that runs down to David (4:17–22), so its first readers knew of King David. Who they were depends on the date. They may have been Judah under David or Solomon, about 1000–930 BC. They may have been Judah late in the monarchy, about 700–600 BC. Or they may have been the Jews of Yehud, a small Persian province, after the return from exile in the 400s BC.
audience.why: To show God's quiet care working through ordinary loyalty (hesed). A Moabite widow is faithful to her Israelite mother-in-law. A landowner keeps the law's kindness to the poor and the foreigner. Together they become the family of Israel's greatest king. Knowing the audience changes the reading. Under David, the book defends a king with a Moabite great-grandmother, and shows his family line as honorable and guided by God. Late in the monarchy, it holds up an older ideal of kindness to the widow and the outsider. After the exile, it reads as a quiet answer to the bans on foreign wives in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13: the Moabite who joins Israel is David's ancestor.
views: The Talmud says that Samuel wrote the book (Bavli Bava Batra 14b). Few hold this now, because the book ends with David, who became king after Samuel died.
Written in the time of the kings

Many traditional and some critical scholars, such as Robert Hubbard and Daniel Block, think it was written under David or Solomon or soon after. It would honor David's family and answer anyone who held his Moabite great-grandmother against him.
Frederic Bush argues from the Hebrew grammar and vocabulary that the book belongs to the late monarchy or the time just after it. On this view its readers were Judah near the end of the kingdom.
Many scholars, such as André LaCocque, date it to the Persian period. They read it as a quiet answer to the bans on foreign wives in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13.
Others think the date cannot be fixed. They think the book was kept because it shows how God's people should treat the widow, the poor and the outsider.

authorship: The Talmud says that "Samuel wrote his book, Judges and Ruth" (Bava Batra 14b). Many Jewish and Christian readers held this view for centuries. Few scholars hold it today, because the book ends with David, who became king after Samuel died, and 4:7 explains an old custom for later readers.

Many scholars, especially conservative ones (Robert Hubbard; Daniel Block, who allows a somewhat later date), think it was written under David or Solomon or soon after, to show that David's family was honorable and chosen by God. They point to the book's classical Hebrew style, its interest in David and not in later kings, and its friendly view of Moab, which would fit David's own ties to Moab (1 Samuel 22:3–4).
Some scholars, such as Frederic Bush, argue from the Hebrew grammar and vocabulary that it belongs to the late monarchy or the time just after it.

Many critical scholars (for example André LaCocque) date it after the exile, partly because of possible late words and Aramaic influence, and read it as a quiet protest against the ban on foreign wives in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13. Others answer that the book never mentions those issues, and that its language is better explained as old, regional or deliberately old-fashioned.
outline: Famine, flight to Moab and three deaths
The road back: Orpah returns, Ruth clings; Naomi comes home "empty"
Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, who protects and feeds her
Naomi's plan; Ruth's request at the threshing floor
The case at the town gate; Boaz redeems the land and marries Ruth
Obed is born; "a son is born to Naomi"
The family line from Perez to David

lenses.name: Jewish
lenses.desc: The synagogue reading at Shavuot. The rabbis (the Talmud, the midrash Ruth Rabbah, the Targum) read Ruth as the model convert and the book as a lesson in hesed, and trace the line to David and the Messiah.

lenses.name: Typology
lenses.desc: Many Christian readers, from the early church to today, see Boaz the redeemer as a picture of Christ, Ruth as a picture of the Gentile church joining God's people, and Bethlehem as pointing to the birth of Jesus.

lenses.name: Royal
lenses.desc: A true family story written in the early monarchy to show David's roots and God's hand in his rise. Held by many conservative scholars and some critical ones.

lenses.name: After exile
lenses.desc: Many critical scholars date the book after the exile and read it as a quiet answer to Ezra and Nehemiah's ban on foreign wives: a Moabite becomes the model Israelite.

lenses.name: Women
lenses.desc: Feminist and literary readers (Phyllis Trible, Tikva Frymer-Kensky, Richard Bauckham) read the only biblical book driven by two women's choices for its picture of women's courage and survival in a man's world.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), aiming for about an 8th-grade reading level. It keeps the book's repeated key words where English can: "go back" (shuv), "faithful love" (hesed), "family redeemer" (go'el), "wing" (kanaf), "worth" (chayil), "rest," "empty" and "stick close" or "cling" (dabaq). Names are spelled as in most English Bibles.

KJV, ASV, WEB, YLT

Public-domain English versions. The KJV (1611, standard text of 1769) prints words the translators added in italics. Young's Literal Translation (1898) keeps Hebrew word order and tenses.

BSB

The Berean Standard Bible, a modern translation released into the public domain.

Hebrew

The Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), the oldest complete Hebrew Bible, as edited by the Westminster Leningrad Codex project and corrected in STEPBible's TAHOT (Tyndale House, Cambridge), with each word's meaning and grammar.

Ruth is a story, and it rewards slow reading. Most of it is dialogue: about two-thirds of its 85 verses contain speech. Watch for words that come back: "return" in chapter 1, "wing" in 2:12 and 3:9, "empty" in 1:21 and 3:17, "worth" in 2:1, 3:11 and 4:11, "rest" in 1:9 and 3:1, "redeemer" all through chapters 2–4. The storyteller rarely comments; you have to notice the echoes.

The book is built in four scenes, one per chapter, each ending with a short exchange between Naomi and Ruth or the women, and each moving from a problem toward its answer: no food becomes a harvest, no husband becomes a marriage, no son becomes a grandson, and no king becomes David.

In Christian Bibles, following the Greek Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate, Ruth comes right after Judges, because it is set "in the days when the judges ruled" (1:1), and before 1 Samuel, which tells of David's rise. In the Hebrew Bible it is among the Writings, the third part of the canon. The Talmud lists it first among the Writings, before Psalms (Bava Batra 14b), perhaps because it leads up to David, the psalmist. In the Leningrad Codex and the scholarly editions based on it (BHS, BHQ) it follows Proverbs, right after the poem about "a woman of worth" (Proverbs 31:10), and Ruth is the woman Boaz calls exactly that (3:11). Many Jewish printed Bibles instead place the five festival scrolls in the order of the festivals, with Ruth after the Song of Songs. It is read at Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks.

Josephus retells the story in his Jewish Antiquities (5.318–337). In the New Testament, Ruth is named once, in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:5).

The Hebrew text of Ruth is well preserved. Four small Dead Sea Scroll copies survive from Qumran (2QRuth-a, 2QRuth-b, 4QRuth-a, 4QRuth-b), from roughly the first century BC to the first century AD; they agree closely with the Masoretic Text, with a few spelling differences. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, is close to the Hebrew too, with a few small additions that explain the story (1:14; 4:8).

The Masoretic Text of Ruth has about a dozen Ketiv/Qere notes, places where the scribes kept the written letters but told readers to say something else. Most are spelling, but two (2:1 and 4:5) affect meaning, and 4:5 is the hardest verse in the book. The differences that matter are listed under "Manuscript differences."

Faithful love (hesed). The book shows loyal love at every level: Ruth to Naomi, Boaz to Ruth and Naomi, and God to all of them. A rabbi said the book was written "to teach how great is the reward of those who do hesed" (Ruth Rabbah 2:14).

Redemption. The family redeemer (go'el) buys back what was lost and keeps a family's name alive. The same word describes God as Israel's redeemer (Isaiah 41:14; 43:1).

The foreigner. A Moabite, from a people the Law kept at a distance (Deuteronomy 23:3), becomes the model of faithfulness and an ancestor of David.

God's hidden care. God does not speak or appear. He works through harvests, "chance" and the choices of ordinary people.

From empty to full. Famine becomes harvest, death becomes birth, bitterness becomes blessing.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians have read Ruth
sections.b:
For Jews, Ruth is the model of the sincere convert who takes on the Torah out of love, and the book is read at Shavuot, when the giving of the Torah at Sinai is remembered. Rabbinic writers also stress Boaz's righteousness and the line from Ruth to David and to the Messiah, son of David.

Christians have read Ruth as a story of grace for the outsider, of a redeemer who pays the price, and of the family line that leads to Bethlehem and to Jesus (Matthew 1:5; Luke 2:4). Many see Boaz as a picture of Christ and Ruth as a picture of the church drawn from the nations. Modern scholars of every background have also admired it as one of the finest short stories in ancient literature.

spec.title: A book about filling what Judges emptied
spec.body: The idea that Ruth answers the end of Judges is widely published (for example by Daniel Block, and by Tod Linafelt, who reads Ruth as a kind of sequel to Judges). What I add is the claim that each of Judges' last horrors has a specific answer in Ruth. Judges closes with "Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25) and with stories in which a Levite from Bethlehem serves idols (Judges 17–18), a Bethlehem woman is abused and killed (Judges 19), and Israel nearly wipes out a tribe and then kidnaps wives for its survivors (Judges 21). Ruth takes the same era and the same town and fills each gap: a foreign woman chooses Israel's God, a Bethlehem woman is protected at night, and a family nearly wiped out is rebuilt by public, lawful marriage. Ruth also answers Judges' refrain about having no king by ending with the name David. I also think the book was placed after Judges in the Greek order not only for its date but because it reads as the answer to Judges' questions.

prompts: Ruth clings to Naomi on the road (1:14–16)

Three women on a dusty road climbing from the Moabite plateau, the Dead Sea far below in haze. An older widow in dark mourning clothes, Naomi, walks toward the west; a young woman, Orpah, turns back toward Moab with her face in her hands; another young woman, Ruth, holds Naomi's arm tightly with both hands. Bundles of belongings, a water skin, sandals; low hills, a few stone walls.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.
Gleaning in the field of Boaz (2:3–9)

A barley field at harvest near the hill town of Bethlehem. Male reapers with sickles cut grain; young women bind the stalks into sheaves; a young foreign woman, Ruth, gleans behind them, gathering stray stalks into her skirt. An older landowner, Boaz, arrives from the town, raising his hand in greeting; a foreman points toward Ruth. Clay water jars in the shade of a simple shelter of branches.

Night on an open threshing floor outside a hill town: a large heap of winnowed barley, a wooden winnowing fork, a few oil lamps going out. A man, Boaz, has just woken and sits up, startled; a young woman, Ruth, kneels at his feet, holding up the corner of his cloak. Stars and a crescent moon above; the dark shapes of other sleeping workers far off.

The sandal at the town gate (4:1–10)

A stone town gate with benches along its inner walls. Ten bearded elders sit in a row; townspeople crowd behind. One man hands his sandal to Boaz, who stands holding it up for all to see. Morning light; farmers with tools passing through the gate toward the fields.

An older woman, Naomi, sits on a low stool holding a newborn boy close in her lap, smiling; a young mother, Ruth, rests nearby; neighbor women gather around, one raising her hands in blessing. Above them, faintly, a branching family tree drawn like a vine, ending in a small shepherd's harp for David.

reading: Robert L. Hubbard Jr., The Book of Ruth (NICOT, 1988)
A thorough evangelical commentary, strong on law, custom and theology.
Frederic W. Bush, Ruth, Esther (Word Biblical Commentary, 1996)
Detailed work on the Hebrew text, with a careful argument about the date.
A classic scholarly commentary, rich on ancient background and on the story's art.
Tamara Cohn Eskenazi and Tikva Frymer-Kensky, Ruth (JPS Bible Commentary, 2011)
A Jewish commentary that brings together rabbinic tradition and modern scholarship.
Daniel I. Block, Judges, Ruth (New American Commentary, 1999)
Reads Ruth in close connection with Judges.
A philological and folklore-based study, full of fresh observations.
Phyllis Trible, God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978)
Its chapter on Ruth, "A Human Comedy," is a landmark of feminist literary reading.
Argues that Ruth is a subversive book written after the exile.
Robert D. Holmstedt, Ruth: A Handbook on the Hebrew Text (2010)
For readers learning Hebrew: every phrase explained.

traditions.q: Should Christians read Ruth for a spiritual sense beyond the story, such as Boaz as a picture of Christ?
views: Yes. Scripture has a literal sense and a spiritual sense, which includes the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses, all resting on the literal (Catechism 115–119). Boaz and Ruth can rightly picture Christ and the Church.
Yes. The fathers read the whole Old Testament through Christ, and the church's hymns keep this way of reading alive. Ruth's place in Christ's family line (Matthew 1:5) is part of the book's meaning.

The plain, historical sense comes first, and Luther warned against fanciful allegories (Lectures on Genesis). Yet Luther found Christ throughout the Old Testament, and Lutherans read Ruth as showing God's grace to a foreigner in Christ's own family line.

Scripture has one true and full sense, not many (Westminster Confession 1.9). Reformed readers may see Boaz as a type of Christ the Redeemer where the Bible's own patterns support it, but reject allegories built on small details.

The Bible should be read in its plain, grammatical and historical sense (Charles Ryrie). Ruth is first a true history of God's care and of David's line; a typology of Christ may illustrate it but is not its meaning.
